t: Introduction: topic and aim of the session
n: This session is devoted to an introduction to medical law. Formerly, it was considered sufficient to observe medical knowledge, skills and moral rules. Now it is also necessary to know the legal norms and to follow them consistently. In current legislation, medical activity in the broad sense is equated with providing services to citizens: the worker is regarded as the service provider and the patient as the consumer. In the view of N. I. Amosov, one should trust the doctor's conscience, and no law can replace it. But law and morality cannot be set against each other. Outline of the session: Chapter 1, the subject of medical law; Chapter 2, foundations of health care legislation; Chapter 3, reform of the health care system.

t: The concept of medical law
n: Medical law is a body of rules and norms regulating the relations of the patient, worker, citizen and institution in diagnosis, treatment and prevention. It defines the scope of the rights, obligations and responsibility of the parties; here the documents regulating general legal and organisational relations are meant. Scope: treatment and preventive care, sanitary and anti-epidemic measures, and other activity in this direction. Attention: there is a risk of error! Moral and ethical demands are fulfilled voluntarily, whereas legal norms are secured directly or indirectly by compulsion.

t: Aim, tasks and skills of the discipline
n: Aim and tasks of the discipline. The student must be aware of the foundations of legislation and the rights and obligations of the worker and the patient. He must be able to analyse medical documents and distinguish defects in medical care. Practical skill: taking part in an official inquiry and in a forensic medical examination as a specialist or expert. The discipline has four tasks. A, studying the foundations of legislation. B, studying the features of legal relations. C, becoming acquainted with professional offences. D, distinguishing a misdemeanour from a crime.

t: Medical activity: a service relationship
n: Medical activity is regarded as a service relationship. In current legislation, medical activity in the broad sense is equated with providing services to citizens. In this, medical staff are interpreted as service providers and patients as consumers. Formerly, medical knowledge and observance of moral rules were considered sufficient; now knowledge of legal norms is also necessary. That is, formerly medical knowledge and skills, and observance of moral and ethical rules, were required, whereas now one must know the legal norms and follow them consistently.

t: Law and morality-ethics: their relation
n: The relation of law and morality-ethics. Amosov: one should trust the doctor's conscience; no law can replace it. Popov, however, stresses that the moral-ethical and legal aspects are interconnected and cannot be set against each other. By level, law is the minimum of morality, and ethics is its higher level. Law is secured by compulsion and does not contradict ethics. Ethics is fulfilled freely, voluntarily, and does not contradict law.

t: Subject of the discipline and special laws
n: Subject of the discipline and special laws. The subject of the discipline is the legal relations in medical activity and the norms defining the legal status of their participants. In first place stands the Constitution, then the special laws: "On the Protection of Citizens' Health" and "On State Sanitary Supervision". There are also laws on medicines, narcotic drugs, HIV prevention, psychiatric care, radiation safety, tuberculosis and blood donation. The everyday activity of staff is also affected by the requirements of civil, labour, administrative and criminal law; these norms also belong to the system of medical law.

t: Case analysis: law and morality
n: Case analysis: law and morality. Situation: a patient seeks medical care. In legislation he is regarded as a consumer, and the doctor as a service provider. Formerly, medical knowledge and observance of moral and ethical rules were considered sufficient. Now it is necessary to know the legal norms and to follow them consistently. Moral and ethical demands are fulfilled voluntarily. Legal norms, however, are secured directly or indirectly by compulsion. Question: why can one not rely on conscience alone? Recall that law is the minimum of morality, and morality is its higher level.

t: The Constitution: foundation of the right to health
n: The Constitution is the foundation of the right to health. Articles 18–20: citizens are equal; the use of rights must not prejudice the interests of others. Article 40 gives the right to qualified medical service; under Article 43 the state creates conditions for this. Article 44 is about judicial protection. Article 45: minors, persons unfit for work and lonely elderly people are under the protection of the state. In the table, Articles 18–20 show equality and the interdependence of right and duty, Article 40 the right to medical service, Article 43 the state guarantee, and Articles 44–45 judicial protection and protection of vulnerable groups.

t: The Constitution: essence of Articles 18–20
n: Let us consider the essence of Articles 18–20 of the Constitution. Article 18: citizens are equal regardless of sex, race, nationality, language and religion; privileges must accord with social justice. The rights and freedoms established by law are inviolable; they may be taken away or restricted only by a court decision. Article 19: the rights and duties of citizens and the state are interconnected. Article 20: the exercise of rights and freedoms must not prejudice the legitimate interests of others.

t: Interrelation of right, obligation and responsibility
n: Right, obligation and responsibility are interconnected. Possession of rights and freedoms presupposes certain duties and obligations. Chapter XI is devoted to duties; failure to observe them is a ground for liability. The chain is as follows: rights established by law, duty and obligations, failure to perform the duty, and liability established by law. Attention: perceive right, obligation and responsibility not separately but as closely linked to one another.

t: Structure of the Law "On the Protection of Citizens' Health"
n: Structure of the Law "On the Protection of Citizens' Health". The Law was adopted by the Oliy Majlis on 29 August 1996. It came into force on 14 September of the same year. The Law consists of 6 parts and 47 articles. Amendments and additions have since been made. Part I covers general provisions, Part II the legal protection of health, Part III medical and social care for citizens, while Parts IV–VI include expert examination, workers and final provisions. The norms of the Law are of a general character. Particular aspects are covered more broadly in sectoral regulatory documents.

t: Tasks of the Law and factors of health
n: Tasks of the Law and factors of health. Article 2: state guarantee of rights, a healthy lifestyle, legal regulation of the activity of bodies. Factors influencing human health: lifestyle 48–52 per cent, heredity 18–20 per cent, environmental factors 18–20 per cent, and medical care 8–10 per cent. Consequently, medical care can provide only about a tenth of health. Attention: medical care is not the main factor of health; first of all the individual himself is responsible.

t: Basic principles of health protection
n: Basic principles of health protection. Article 3 gives five principles: observance of human rights, use of care by all strata of the population, and the priority of prevention. The other two principles: social protection of the citizen on loss of health, and the unity of medical science with practice. Powers: the Cabinet of Ministers, Article 4; the Ministry of Health, Article 5; local authorities, Article 6. Article 7 covers the systems: state, private and others. Remember: R-A-P-S-S: Rights, Access, Prevention, Social protection, Science and practice. This is a study aid.

t: Health care systems and free care
n: Health care systems and free care. The Law distinguishes state, private and other health care systems, as given in Article 7. State institutions provide guaranteed medical care free of charge; its scope and procedure are established by legislation. Medical and other services beyond the guarantee are considered additional, and the citizen pays for them; this is in Article 8. Primary care in the state system is provided free of charge, with a state guarantee, whereas in the private system it is mainly under contract. For certain groups it is free here as well. The procedure for the groups is determined by the Cabinet of Ministers.

t: Quick question: foundations of the Constitution and the Law
n: Quick questions. First question: which article of the Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to use qualified medical service? Second question: when was the Law "On the Protection of Citizens' Health" adopted, and of how many parts and articles does it consist? Third question: list the 5 basic principles of health protection in the Law. What care is free in the state system? Attention: Article 18 of the Constitution is about equality, whereas Article 18 of the Law is about free consultation for the family. Distinguish them!

t: Rights of the family and special categories
n: Rights of the family and special categories. Article 18: in state institutions the citizen receives free consultation on the family, on whether a dangerous disease is present, and on the medical-psychological and medical-genetic aspects of marriage and the family. Each family chooses its family doctor itself; families with children enjoy the benefits established by legislation. The medical examination of those entering marriage is established by Article 17 of the Family Code and Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 365 of 25 August 2003; this corresponds to Article 18 of the Law. Special categories: persons of certain professions, Article 17; minors, 19; military personnel, 20; pensioners, 21; disabled persons, 22; those affected by emergencies, Article 23.

t: Protection from discrimination and the family doctor
n: Protection from discrimination and the family doctor. The state ensures the inviolability of citizens' health rights regardless of age, sex, race, nationality, language, religion and social status. It is guaranteed that the state protects citizens from discrimination irrespective of any form of illness; this is in Article 13. Article 18: free consultation and examination on family matters, on whether a dangerous disease is present, and on the medical-psychological and medical-genetic aspects of marriage and the family. Each family chooses its family doctor itself; families with children enjoy the benefits established by legislation.

t: Patient's rights (Article 24)
n: Patient's rights, Article 24. The patient may demand respectful and humane treatment from medical staff. He chooses the doctor and the treatment and preventive institution himself. Examination, treatment and care take place in conditions that meet sanitary-hygienic requirements. At his request a consilium is held and another specialist gives advice. The fact of the visit, the state of health and the diagnosis are kept confidential. The patient gives consent to a medical procedure of his own will or refuses it. Harm is compensated in the lawful manner; an advocate or representative is engaged for protection. If a right is violated, a complaint is lodged with the management, a higher body or the court.

t: Right to information (Article 25)
n: Right to information, Article 25. The citizen has the right to full information on the results of examination and treatment, the diagnosis and the prognosis of the disease. He is also told about the methods of treatment, their risks, the possible types of procedures and the consequences. Attention: information about persons under 14 and those declared lacking capacity is given not to the patient himself but to the legal representative. If an unfavourable course of the disease is anticipated, the information is communicated to the citizen or the person he designates, observing the norms of medical ethics.

t: Consent to medical intervention (Article 26)
n: Consent to medical intervention, Article 26. Medical intervention is carried out only with the voluntary consent of the informed citizen. For persons under 14 and those declared lacking capacity, the legal representative gives consent. If there is no representative, the matter is decided by a consilium, and if one is not assembled, by the attending or duty doctor. The procedure is as follows: first voluntary consent; for persons under 14 and those lacking capacity, the legal representative; if there is no representative or the patient cannot express his will, a consilium; if a consilium is not assembled, the decision of the attending or duty doctor; then the management of the institution is informed.

t: Refusal and care without consent (Articles 27–28)
n: Refusal and care without consent, Articles 27–28. The patient or his legal representative may refuse medical intervention or demand that it be stopped. Refusal is formalised by written confirmation, or if that is not possible, a report is drawn up in the presence of witnesses. If a representative has refused and the consequences are severe, the guardianship authority is informed. If the disease is dangerous to those around, consent is not required: examination, hospitalisation, observation and isolation are possible.

t: Types of medical and social care (Articles 29–31)
n: Types of medical and social care, Articles 29–31. Part 3 of the Law gives the types of care: primary, urgent and emergency, and specialised. Primary care in state institutions is regarded as the basic, accessible and free type of service; its scope and procedure are determined by the Ministry. The right to receive urgent care exists in all institutions, as stated in Article 30. Specialised care requires special methods and complex technology; its type, scope and standard are determined by the Ministry. Attention: in private institutions primary care is mainly under contract, and free for certain groups; the groups and scope are determined by the Cabinet of Ministers.

t: Composition of primary health care (Article 29)
n: Composition of primary health care, Article 29. Primary care is the basic, accessible and free type of service in the state system. Composition: treatment of common diseases, injuries, poisonings and other urgent conditions. Also sanitary-hygienic and anti-epidemic measures and medical prevention of the most important diseases. This also includes measures related to protecting the family, motherhood and childhood and providing primary care at the place of residence. The scope and procedure are determined by the Ministry of Health.

t: Emergency care and socially significant diseases
n: Emergency care and socially significant diseases. Article 30: citizens have the right to emergency medical care in all treatment and preventive institutions. If life is in danger, medical staff may use any transport to take the patient to the institution. Until medical staff arrive, primary care must be given by the police, fire service, emergency service and transport workers. Resolution No. 153, 20 March 1997: tuberculosis, oncological diseases, sexually transmitted diseases, mental illnesses, leprosy and AIDS are regarded as socially significant.

t: Quick question: patient's rights and types of care
n: Quick question: patient's rights and types of care. Question: a 12-year-old child needs medical intervention. Who gives consent? Can the patient himself? Answer: for persons under 14 and those declared lacking legal capacity, consent is given by their legal representatives. Attention: if will cannot be expressed and the intervention cannot be delayed, a consilium; if one is not assembled, the attending or duty doctor decides and the management is informed. If the patient refuses the intervention, the doctor obtains written confirmation of refusal. If that is not possible, a report is drawn up in the presence of witnesses.

t: Types of medical expert examination (Articles 36–40)
n: Types of medical expert examination, Articles 36–40. The fourth part of the Law gives the various forms of medical expert examination. Articles 36–37 concern temporary incapacity and medical-labour expert examination. Article 38 concerns military-medical, Article 39 forensic medical and forensic psychiatric, and Article 40 pathoanatomical examination. Pathoanatomical examination received for the first time in legislation the status of a type of medical expert examination. The procedure for this examination and for establishing the time of death is determined by the Ministry of Health.

t: Medical workers: diploma and licence
n: Medical workers: diploma and licence. Only persons holding a diploma of the relevant higher or secondary specialised educational institution engage in this activity; this is in Article 41. For certain types, a diploma and a licence determined by the Ministry are required. Private practice is conducted with a diploma and a licence for the chosen type; the licence may be suspended by the issuing body or by a court decision. Quality control is carried out by associations, the authorities and the Ministry, as in Article 42. Workers may form voluntary professional associations and protect their rights through them; this is in Article 43.

t: Tasks of professional associations (Article 43)
n: Tasks of professional associations, Article 43. Medical and pharmaceutical workers may, on a voluntary basis, form professional associations and other public associations. Task: developing medical and pharmaceutical practice and supporting scientific research. Also protecting the rights of workers and resolving other questions related to professional activity. The quality of private practice is monitored by professional associations, local authorities and the body that issued the licence; this is in Article 42.

t: The doctor's oath and medical confidentiality
n: The doctor's oath and medical confidentiality. Article 44: the text of the oath of a doctor of the Republic of Uzbekistan is given. It is taken by those graduating from a higher medical educational institution and receiving a doctor's diploma. Legislation establishes corresponding liability for cases where doctors violate the oath. Article 45: information on seeking care, state of health, diagnosis, examination and treatment is medical confidentiality; it is not disclosed without the consent of the citizen or representative. If the secret is conveyed to other persons in the permitted manner, they too, like medical staff, must keep it. Liability is provided for violation.

t: Exceptions to medical confidentiality
n: Exceptions to medical confidentiality. As an exception, disclosing the secret without the consent of the citizen or legal representative is possible in 6 cases. First case: persons under 14, in which case parents or the representative are informed. Second: persons lacking capacity, the legal representative being informed. Third: a patient unable to express his will, for the purpose of examination and treatment. Fourth: an infectious disease or mass poisoning dangerous to those around. Fifth: an official request, that is, one coming from the bodies of inquiry, investigation, the prosecutor's office and the court. Sixth: unlawful harm. Article 241 of the Criminal Code: failure to report and concealment entail criminal liability; report officially.

t: Compensation of harm and liability (Article 46)
n: Compensation of harm and liability, Article 46. Harm caused to a citizen's life and health through the worker's improper performance of official duties is compensated. The harm is compensated in the manner established by legislative acts. Compensation of harm does not release the worker from disciplinary, administrative and criminal liability. The requirements of the Law are of a general character; particular aspects are covered more precisely and broadly in sectoral regulatory documents.

t: Case analysis: consent and medical confidentiality
n: Case analysis: consent and medical confidentiality. Situation: a 10-year-old child in serious condition is brought in, needing an urgent procedure, and there are no parents. Who decides? For a child under 14, consent to the intervention is given by the legal representative. If there is no representative, a consilium decides, and if one is not assembled, the attending or duty doctor. Medical confidentiality is disclosed without consent in exceptional cases: to the parents of a child under 14, where there is a danger to those around, and on the official request of the investigation or court. Attention: failure to report, or concealment of, harm resulting from an unlawful act entails liability under Article 241 of the Criminal Code.

t: Need for reform: shortcomings of the old system
n: Now we turn to the reform of the health care system. The need for reform arises from the shortcomings of the old system. The primary level was built on the district-territorial principle: at first one general practitioner-therapist worked, then narrow specialists were added. In the countryside, weak institutions without qualified specialists multiplied: feldsher-midwife posts, rural medical outpatient clinics, district hospitals. The financing mechanism was not fully formed, while the number of jobs grew. As a result expenditure rose and the quality of care fell. Patients who could have been treated at a polyclinic were often admitted to hospital. This increased the number of hospital beds without modern equipment.

t: State programme: aim, principles and tasks
n: State programme: aim, principles and tasks. Aim: to build a system that creates conditions for protecting the health of the population and bringing up a healthy generation. Principles: equal access to services, the priority of prevention, market mechanisms and private practice. Task: strengthening the system of primary and emergency care, and a stage-by-stage transition to the general practitioner. Stages of the documents: Resolution No. 182 of 1996, for the countryside; the Presidential Decree dated 10.11.1998; the State Programme for 1998–2005, in which the aim, principles and tasks are defined.

t: Financing: free and paid services
n: Financing: free and paid services. The state guarantees free provision of emergency care, vaccination, childbirth care and examination of children. Examination of non-residents and of the mandatory-screening contingent is paid under contract, whereas emergency care is free. Non-state institutions provide free services to preferential patients to the extent of up to 20% of their activity. According to the table, emergency care, ambulance care and vaccination are free from the state budget; for tuberculosis, oncological and psychiatric diseases specialised care is free; state funds are allocated for prevention, personnel and scientific research.

t: Rebuilding the primary level
n: Rebuilding the primary level. Primary care is the foundation of the system; about 90% of consultations can be resolved at this level. In per capita financing there is a single norm for each person; more is allocated for women of childbearing age and children. A financial manager has been introduced into the staff of the post: he handles the reserve, settlements and reporting. The difference between the old and new systems: there were five tiers, now there are two. In the countryside, a rural medical post in place of the feldsher-midwife post. Financing is not by number of staff, floor area and visits, but by the per capita norm. A general practitioner in place of narrow specialists.

t: Emergency care, medical education and the private sector
n: Emergency care, medical education and the private sector. The Republican Scientific Centre of Emergency Care, its regional branches, and district and city departments operate; the system also includes emergency medical services and sanitary aviation. Higher medical education has two stages: general practitioners are trained in the bachelor's programme, and specialists in the relevant fields in the master's programme. A Centre for the licensing and attestation of doctors and pharmacists has been established under the Ministry of Health. Private practice is being expanded, but the principle of universal free care guaranteed by the state must not be violated.

t: Decrees of 2003 and 2007
n: Decrees of 2003 and 2007. The Decree, taking foreign experience into account, envisaged creating specialised clinics and medical centres. The Decree of 2007 opened six new centres, including centres of paediatrics, endocrinology and phthisiology. The creation of regional multi-profile centres and district medical associations is envisaged. Documents: the Decree of 26 February 2003, the second stage and four pilot centres; the Decree of 19 September 2007, six new centres; district associations provide coordination and methodological assistance; the Resolution of 2 October 2007 concerns improving management.

t: Case analysis and quick question: reform
n: Case analysis and quick question: reform. Situation: a primary institution is financed according to the number of attached population. More funds are allocated for women of childbearing age and children. Formerly, funds were given by the number of staff, floor area and visits. It was more convenient for doctors to send a patient to hospital. Quick question: why was the primary level strengthened? Effective primary care can satisfy about 90% of consultations, and hospital admissions decrease. Attention: there is a risk of error. Per capita financing is not financing by number of staff.

t: Conclusion: key conclusions and review questions
n: Conclusion and review questions. Article 40 of the Constitution gives the right to qualified medical service. The Law sets the general provisions, and sectoral documents the details. The ultimate aim is for all strata of the population to use qualified service. For this, resources must be used effectively and workers must be qualified. Knowing the Law and sectoral documents raises the legal literacy and culture of medical staff. Review questions: which article gives the right to medical service? What are the main principles of health care legislation and the principles of the reform?
